title: Metzora: empty the house first (Leviticus 14:33–36)
hook: even walls can be afflicted; the house is emptied first to spare the owner's things

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, a living bird flew free over an open field. Your line was let the bird go. Did you open your hands on an old grievance? Today, the affliction moves into the walls. Day four hundred three.

Black mold behind the bathroom tiles is its own kind of bad news. Something is wrong with the house itself, the place that was supposed to be safe. Leviticus 14 imagines something like it. A homeowner notices greenish or reddish streaks sunk into the stone. He goes to the priest and says, carefully, something like a plague has appeared in my house. Before the priest even steps through the door, the Torah gives an instruction that has nothing to do with stone at all.
screen: `MOLD BEHIND THE TILES.` → `STREAKS IN THE STONE.` → `BEFORE THE PRIEST GOES IN.`

segments.voice: Start with the instruction. The priest commands that the house be emptied before he goes in to look. Why? Because once he declares the house unclean, everything still inside becomes unclean with it. Then, whose sake it's for. The Mishnah asks what would be lost, and answers: clothes and wood can be washed or purified, but earthenware pots can't. They'd have to be broken. And the Mishnah draws a principle from that: the Torah has concern for people's property. Before it rules on the walls, it saves the dishes. Rashi adds a surprise. Rashi passes on an old midrash about why the walls were struck at all. The Amorites, it says, hid their gold in the walls of their houses during the forty years Israel was in the desert. A plague on the wall meant the stones came out, and the owner found treasure. An affliction that turns out to be a gift. It's a story, a midrash, not something the verse says. And an honest note. A rabbinic opinion in the Talmud says a plagued house never actually happened and never will; it was written to be studied. Other rabbis answered that they knew of places where it had. The sources disagree, and they leave the disagreement standing. Whichever view you take, the verse keeps its order: empty it first. Take care of what matters before the verdict, because the verdict, whatever it is, shouldn't destroy more than it has to.
screen: `EMPTY THE HOUSE BEFORE HE LOOKS.` · `SAVE THE CLAY POTS.` · `THE GOLD IN THE WALLS.` · `NEVER HAPPENED, OR DID IT?` · then, large: `EMPTY IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear out one corner. Settle, and breathe. Picture one corner of your home that's been quietly building up. A drawer, a closet shelf, the chair that collects clothes. Picture emptying it, item by item, onto the floor. Which things do you want to save? Which have you been keeping only because you never looked? Later today, if you can, go and actually do it. One corner, emptied first, then looked at with fresh eyes. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion where even a house can be afflicted, and the priest has it emptied first, to spare the owner's things.
Your line: empty it first. Today, before you deal with a problem, take a minute to protect what doesn't need to be lost. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: The laws of afflicted houses are studied in the Mishnah's tractate Negaim and in the weekly reading of Metzora; the principle that the Torah has concern for people's property is cited in later Jewish law.

fork.reveal: empty it first. Leviticus 14:36 protects the owner's things before the verdict on the walls.

original.note: Hebrew: "and they shall empty the house" (Leviticus 14:36).

trapdoor: what you thought: rules about mold.
what it means: even in a ruling about walls, the Torah stops to save the owner's things.

what a scholar hears: Mishnah Negaim 12:5 says the Torah has concern for Israel's property; Sanhedrin 71a records the view that a plagued house never was, and the reply that some knew where one stood.

notes: Lev 14:37 describes the streaks as greenish or reddish (yerakrakot or adamdamot); confirm wording.
Mishnah Negaim 12:5 (the Torah has concern for Israel's property; earthenware cannot be purified) cited from memory; confirm.
Rashi 14:34, from Vayikra Rabbah 17:6: Amorites hid treasure in walls during the 40 years in the desert. Confirm.
Sanhedrin 71a: 'a leprous house never was and never will be'; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok cite places where one stood. Confirm names before they're named.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Rashi on 14:34 names the Amorites, not the Canaanites; corrected in the teach and the match game; the plagued stones are removed (14:40), not the whole wall; hook no longer tells the listener what they feel; "what all the readings share" overstated and is reworded; removed the ordinal scaffold.
